'''Shota Rustaveli Tbilisi International Airport''' ({{lang-ka|თბილისის შოთა რუსთაველის სახელობის საერთაშორისო აეროპორტი}}) {{airport codes|TBS|UGTB}} is the busiest [[international airport]] in [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]], located {{convert|17|km|abbr=on}} southeast of capital [[Tbilisi]]. The airport handled 4.75 million passengers in 2024. The airport is operated by [[TAV Airports Holding]], making it a part of [[Groupe ADP]].

Over 45 airlines operate from the airport, with nonstop or direct flights to over 25 countries.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://tbilisiairport.com/en-EN/flights/page/airport-route-map |title=Airport Route Map |publisher=Tbilisi International Airport |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20240329144533/https://tbilisiairport.com/en-EN/flights/page/airport-route-map |archivedate=29 March 2024 |accessdate=7 April 2024 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://tbilisiairport.com/en-EN/flights/page/airlines |title=Airlines |publisher=Tbilisi International Airport |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20231003115529/https://tbilisiairport.com/en-EN/flights/page/airlines |archivedate=3 October 2023 |accessdate=7 April 2024 }}</ref>

Tbilisi Airport is a hub for [[Georgian Airways]], flag carrier of Georgia, as well as for [[MyWay Airlines]] and [[Camex (airline)|Camex]].

In 2015, [[Tbilisi City Assembly]] named the airport after medieval Georgian poet [[Shota Rustaveli]] (1160–1220).<ref>{{cite news |url=https://ghn.ge/news/133823 |title=თბილისის საერთაშორისო აეროპორტს შოთა რუსთაველის სახელი მიენიჭა |language=Ka |trans-title=Tbilisi International Airport was named after Shota Rustaveli |work=GHN |date=30 June 2015 |accessdate=7 April 2024 }}</ref>

==General==
Tbilisi Airport is home to Georgian flag carrier [[Georgian Airways]] and [[MyWay Airlines]], which was founded in 2017. The airport is served by approximately 30 airlines, mainly from [[Europe]], the [[Middle East]], and [[Central Asia]] serving roughly 30 destinations out of Tbilisi. Due to the increasing popularity of Georgia and the city of Tbilisi as a tourist destination, the number of travelers grew since 2010 from 1 million to almost 4 million until the outbreak of the coronavirus pandemic. The airspace of Georgia was closed for most of 2020 with the exception of government-mandated expatriation flights,<ref>{{cite news | url=https://agenda.ge/en/news/2021/264 | title=Georgia resumes regular flights today | date=1 February 2021 | work=Agenda.ge | access-date=30 November 2021 | archive-date=30 November 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211130181707/https://agenda.ge/en/news/2021/264 | url-status=live }}</ref> but regular international air traffic resumed as of February 2021.

Following a political row in June 2019, Russia banned flights to and from Georgia starting 8 July 2019.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.rferl.org/a/putin-ban-on-direct-russia-georgia-flights-comes-into-force/30042902.html | title=Putin's Ban On Direct Russia-Georgia Flights Comes Into Force | date=8 July 2019 | work=[[Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty]] | access-date=30 November 2021 | archive-date=8 April 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210408000357/https://www.rferl.org/a/putin-ban-on-direct-russia-georgia-flights-comes-into-force/30042902.html | url-status=live }}</ref> Georgian Airways from Tbilisi to [[Vnukovo International Airport|Moscow-Vnukovo]] have since been operated by Aircompany Armenia through Yerevan. The ban was still in effect at the end of 2021. The Kremlin has also banned all Russian airlines from flying to Georgia. A similar ban was in effect during 2006–2008.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.france24.com/en/20080326-moscow-ends-flight-embargo-russia-georgia | title=Moscow ends Georgian flight embargo | date=26 March 2008 | work=[[France 24]] | access-date=30 November 2021 | archive-date=30 November 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211130142959/https://www.france24.com/en/20080326-moscow-ends-flight-embargo-russia-georgia | url-status=live }}</ref>

The [[George W. Bush]] Avenue ([[S5 highway (Georgia)|Kakheti Highway]]) leads from the airport to the center of Tbilisi.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://apnews.com/188837e36fdbe2b14c4d0b615b2e33c5 | title=Tbilisi Officials Name Street After Bush | date=14 September 2005 | work=Associated Press News | access-date=16 January 2023 | archive-date=27 November 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211127091323/https://apnews.com/188837e36fdbe2b14c4d0b615b2e33c5 | url-status=live }}</ref>

==History==
[[File:Foreign Secretary James Cleverly visits Georgia (3).jpg|thumb|left|Terminal of 1952, now VIP lounge]]
[[File:Old Airport Terminal in Tbilisi, built 1968.jpg|thumb|left|Terminal of 1968, now disused]] The first airport terminal building, which functions now as a VIP lounge, was constructed in 1952. Designed in the style of [[Stalinist architecture]], the building featured a floor plan with symmetric axes and a monumental [[avant-corps]] in the form of a [[portico]]. The two wings featured [[blind arcade]]s in [[giant order]]. Second terminal building was completed in 1968, designed by the chief architect Vladimer Beridze and others<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nplg.gov.ge/bios/ka/00003141/|work=Biographical Dictionary of Georgia|access-date=24 February 2026|language=ka|title=ვლადიმერ ბერიძე}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine|url=https://dccollection.share.library.harvard.edu/georgianstudies/files/original/6d15ba3f5ce4defbfbd5a3d04093d4a90cafb61e.pdf|access-date=24 February 2026|date=21 May 1971|magazine=სამშობლო|language=ka|trans-magazine=Samshoblo|title=თბილისი აქედან იწყება...|trans-title=Tbilisi Starts Here...|issue=10 (266)|page=4}}</ref> in the [[International Style]],<ref>{{cite book|last=Baulig|first=Josef |author2=Maia Mania |author3=Hans Mildenberg |author4=Karl Ziegler|title=Architekturführer Tbilisi|publisher=Landeshauptstadt Saarbrücken/Technische Universität Kaiserslautern|pages=70|isbn=3-936890-39-0|language=de, ka|year=2004 }}</ref> now is likewise out of public service.

In 1981 Tbilisi airport was the 12th largest airport in the [[Soviet Union]], with 1,478,000 passengers on so-called central lines, which were flights connecting Tbilisi with cities in other Soviet republics.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Sagers|first=Matthew|author2=Thomas Maraffa |date=July 1990|title=Soviet Air-Passenger Transportation Network|journal=Geographical Review|publisher=American Geographical Society|volume=80|issue=3|pages=269|doi=10.2307/215304|jstor=215304|bibcode=1990GeoRv..80..266S }}</ref> After the dissolution of the Soviet Union, the civil war and the economic crisis in the newly independent Georgia, passenger numbers had dropped to 230,000 by 1998.<ref>{{cite journal|year=1998|publisher=Chartered Institute of Transport in the UK|location=Stroudgate|issue=13–15|page=97}}{{full citation needed|date=May 2024}}</ref>

Tbilisi International Airport is operated by [[TAV Airports Holding]] (TAV) Urban Georgia since October 2005 whose concession has been extended until at least 2027.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.civil.ge/eng/article.php?id=25147|title=Civil.Ge - TAV Gets Tbilisi Airport Operation Extension for Planned USD 65m Investment|author=Civil Georgia|access-date=27 August 2012|archive-date=5 February 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150205011431/http://www.civil.ge/eng/article.php?id=25147|url-status=live}}</ref> In Georgia, the company also operates [[Batumi International Airport]] for a 20-year term since May 2007. [[TAV Airports Holding]], which owns a 76% share in Tbilisi airport operator TAV Urban Georgia, agreed with the Georgian state-owned [[United Airports of Georgia]] to reconstruct and extend the unused runway, one of the two runways at the Tbilisi airport, in line with ICAO standards to accept all types of aircraft, including the Boeing 747-8, Airbus A380-800, Antonov An-225 and Antonov An-124. A new F Code taxiway was also planned.{{citation needed|date=December 2025}}

===Modernisation===
[[file:Departure Hall.jpg|2007 departure lounge|thumb]]
[[file:Interior TBS.jpg|Ground floor check-in area|thumb]] 

February 2007 saw the completion of a US$90.5 million reconstruction project, with the construction of a new international terminal, a car park, improvements to the apron, taxiway and runway and the acquisition of ground handling equipment and an annual passenger capacity of 2.8 million.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://old.civil.ge/eng/article.php?id=14587|title=New Airport Terminal Opened in Tbilisi|date=7 February 2007|access-date=30 November 2020|archive-date=6 May 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210506040232/https://old.civil.ge/eng/article.php?id=14587|url-status=live}}</ref> A rail link to the city centre was constructed, with an infrequent rail service of two trains per day each way. The airport got a contemporary and functional design, to provide an optimized flow of both passengers and luggage from the parking lot to the planes, with a {{convert|25000|m2|abbr=on}} total usable area, while future expansions can be implemented without interrupting terminal operations. Various food and beverage operations have been incorporated in the new terminal, including four duty-free stores. The implementing party for the project was TAV Urban Georgia, a concessionaire and [[Special-purpose entity]] for the construction and operation of the airport, and the project was financed by the [[International Finance Corporation]] (IFC) and [[European Bank for Reconstruction and Development]] (EBRD).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://pressroom.ifc.org/all/pages/PressDetail.aspx?ID=21284|title=IFC and EBRD to Finance TAV's Airport Operations in Georgia|publisher=[[International Finance Corporation]]|date=17 May 2006|access-date=30 November 2021|archive-date=30 November 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211130181707/https://pressroom.ifc.org/all/pages/PressDetail.aspx?ID=21284|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 2016, the main runway of the airport was renovated and equipped with new navigation lighting. Runway guard lights and guidance signs at all the holding positions on the airport's main runway were added. The [[instrument landing system]] was also upgraded. The airfield lighting control and monitoring system was upgraded, including installation of new lighting signals on all four taxiways. In 2017, a new arrival terminal with an area of {{convert|12000|m2}}, integrated with the existing terminal building, was completed to meet the increasing numbers of travelers. The terminal's capacity was increased to 3.5 million passengers per year.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.airport-technology.com/projects/tbilisi-airports-new-arrivals-terminal-tbilisi/|title=Tbilisi Airport's New Arrivals Terminal, Tbilisi, Georgia|publisher=airport-technology.com|date=1 December 2017|access-date=30 November 2021|archive-date=30 November 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211130150350/https://www.airport-technology.com/projects/tbilisi-airports-new-arrivals-terminal-tbilisi/|url-status=live}}</ref> In addition to the expansion of the terminal building, this $33 million project implemented, among other things, a new boarding bridge with two exits, five new aircraft parking spaces, three {{Convert|150|m|adj=on}} luggage racks and a new parking lot for 250 cars.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://gtarchive.georgiatoday.ge/news/7677/New-Terminal-Opens-at-Tbilisi-International-Airport|title=New Terminal Opens at Tbilisi International Airport|publisher=Georgia Today|date=26 September 2017|access-date=30 November 2021|archive-date=30 November 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211130143003/http://gtarchive.georgiatoday.ge/news/7677/New-Terminal-Opens-at-Tbilisi-International-Airport|url-status=live}}</ref>

A new [[Tbilisi Metro]] overground line linking the airport with the city was announced in October 2018. The proposed extension would connect the airport with Samgori metro station as transfer point with the existing metro line. Construction was set to begin in late 2019,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://jam-news.net/a-new-metro-railway-and-electric-cars-promises-made-to-the-georgian-public-a-week-before-elections/|title=A new metro, railway and electric cars: promises made to the Georgian public a week before elections|date=22 October 2018|access-date=31 December 2018|archive-date=31 December 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181231144132/https://jam-news.net/a-new-metro-railway-and-electric-cars-promises-made-to-the-georgian-public-a-week-before-elections/|url-status=live}}</ref> but the project was effectively abandoned in spring 2021 when a feasibility study did not produce the desired outcome.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.interpressnews.ge/ka/article/646717-lilo-samgori-aeroportis-mimartulebit-miciszeda-metros-proektis-ganxorcielebaze-tbilisis-meriam-shesazloa-uari-tkvas/|title=Tbilisi City Hall may refuse to implement overground metro project in the direction of Lilo-Samgori-Airport|date=16 March 2021|publisher=Inter Press News|access-date=30 November 2021|archive-date=30 November 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211130094309/https://www.interpressnews.ge/ka/article/646717-lilo-samgori-aeroportis-mimartulebit-miciszeda-metros-proektis-ganxorcielebaze-tbilisis-meriam-shesazloa-uari-tkvas/|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Accidents==
On 20 July 1992, a [[Tupolev Tu-154]] cargo plane loaded with about 20 tons of tea (carrying more than 2 tons over the weight limit for a safe take-off) [[1992 Tbilisi Tupolev Tu-154 crash|overran the runway and crashed]] during a takeoff attempt, killing all 24 people aboard and 4 on the ground.<ref>{{cite news |title=Accident description |url=https://aviation-safety.net/asndb/325495 |access-date=11 May 2024 |work=Aviation Safety Network}}</ref>

Shota Rustaveli Tbilisi International Airport (Georgian: თბილისის შოთა რუსთაველის სახელობის საერთაშორისო აეროპორტი) (IATA: TBS, ICAO: UGTB) is the busiest international airport in Georgia, located 17 km (11 mi) southeast of capital Tbilisi. The airport handled 4.75 million passengers in 2024. The airport is operated by TAV Airports Holding, making it a part of Groupe ADP.
Over 45 airlines operate from the airport, with nonstop or direct flights to over 25 countries.
Tbilisi Airport is a hub for Georgian Airways, flag carrier of Georgia, as well as for MyWay Airlines and Camex.
In 2015, Tbilisi City Assembly named the airport after medieval Georgian poet Shota Rustaveli (1160–1220).
